subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Plate Tectonics and Natural Hazards Reading
subtitle: Reading passages with comprehension questions on plate motion, boundaries, hazards, and risk.
description: A passage pack for reading practice about plate tectonics and natural hazards. Passages include evidence for plate tectonics, boundary processes, earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis, and community risk reduction.

data.sourceTitle: Why Plate Tectonics Explains Earth Patterns
data.targetTitle: Why Plate Tectonics Explains Earth Patterns
data.sourcePassage: Earth's surface is not one solid shell. It is broken into large tectonic plates that move slowly over the softer asthenosphere. The movement is only a few centimeters each year, but over millions of years it can open oceans, build mountains, and shift continents. Scientists accept plate tectonics because many types of evidence fit together. South America and Africa appear to match like puzzle pieces. Similar fossils and rock layers are found on continents now separated by oceans. On the seafloor, young rocks and matching magnetic stripes appear beside mid-ocean ridges. Earthquake and volcano maps also show long patterns that line up with plate boundaries. GPS measurements confirm that plates are still moving today.

questions.question: What layer do tectonic plates move over?
questions.modelAnswer: They move over the softer asthenosphere.

questions.question: Which observation suggests continents were once joined?
options: South America and Africa seem to fit together
questions.modelAnswer: South America and Africa seem to fit together.

questions.question: Why is GPS evidence important for plate tectonics?
questions.modelAnswer: GPS can measure small changes in position, showing that plates are still moving today.

questions.question: How do earthquake and volcano maps support plate tectonics?
questions.modelAnswer: They show long patterns that line up with plate boundaries, so the hazards are not randomly scattered.

questions.question: Explain why several kinds of evidence are stronger than one observation alone.
questions.modelAnswer: Several independent observations, such as fossils, rocks, seafloor data, hazard patterns, and GPS, all point to the same explanation, making the theory more reliable.

data.sourcePassage: Plate boundaries are places where tectonic plates meet. At divergent boundaries, plates move apart. Magma rises, cools, and forms new crust, often at mid-ocean ridges or rift valleys. At convergent boundaries, plates move toward each other. If an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the denser oceanic plate usually subducts, forming a trench and possibly volcanoes. If two continents collide, the crust crumples and thickens to form large mountains. At transform boundaries, plates slide past each other. Crust is not usually created or destroyed, but rocks can lock, stress can build, and earthquakes can occur. Each boundary type has a different pattern of landforms and hazards.

questions.question: What happens at a divergent boundary?
questions.modelAnswer: Plates move apart.

questions.question: Which plate usually subducts when oceanic crust meets continental crust?
questions.modelAnswer: The denser oceanic plate usually subducts.

questions.question: Why are volcanoes possible at oceanic-continental convergent boundaries?
questions.modelAnswer: The sinking oceanic plate helps mantle rock melt, and the magma can rise to form volcanoes.

questions.question: How is a transform boundary different from a divergent boundary?
questions.modelAnswer: At a transform boundary plates slide past each other and crust is not usually created; at a divergent boundary plates move apart and new crust can form.

questions.question: A region has folded mountains and strong earthquakes but few volcanoes. Which boundary is most likely, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: It is likely a continental-continental convergent boundary because continental crust collides, crumples, thickens, and forms mountains without easy subduction.

data.sourceTitle: Earthquakes and the San Andreas Fault
data.targetTitle: Earthquakes and the San Andreas Fault
data.sourcePassage: An earthquake happens when rocks suddenly move along a fault. Plates may keep trying to move, but friction can cause rocks at the fault to lock. Stress builds until the rocks slip, releasing energy as seismic waves. The focus is the underground point where the earthquake starts, and the epicenter is the point on the surface directly above it. The San Andreas Fault in California is a transform boundary between the Pacific Plate and North American Plate. It does not create a line of volcanoes, but it can create earthquakes. Damage from an earthquake depends on more than magnitude. Depth, distance from the epicenter, ground type, building design, population density, and preparedness all matter.

questions.question: What is the focus of an earthquake?
questions.modelAnswer: The focus is the underground point where the earthquake starts.

questions.question: What type of boundary is the San Andreas Fault?
questions.modelAnswer: Transform boundary.

questions.question: Why can stress build along a fault?
questions.modelAnswer: Friction can lock rocks together while plates keep trying to move, so stress builds until the rocks slip.

questions.question: Why might two places experience different damage from the same magnitude earthquake?
questions.modelAnswer: Damage can differ because of depth, distance, ground type, building design, population density, and preparedness.

questions.question: Explain why transform boundaries are linked strongly to earthquakes but not usually to volcano chains.
questions.modelAnswer: Transform plates slide past each other, so locked faults can release energy as earthquakes, but crust is not usually created, destroyed, or melted to form volcano chains.

data.sourcePassage: Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface as lava, ash, and gases. They are common at subduction zones because a sinking oceanic plate can help mantle rock melt. They also form at divergent boundaries where plates move apart and magma rises to fill the gap. Some volcanoes form at hot spots away from plate boundaries. The Hawaiian Islands formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a hot spot. Tsunamis are another hazard connected to tectonic activity. A tsunami can form when a strong, shallow underwater earthquake causes vertical movement of the seafloor. Water is displaced, waves spread across the ocean, and near shore the waves slow down and grow taller, creating flooding and strong currents.

questions.question: What is lava?
questions.modelAnswer: Lava is melted rock that reaches Earth's surface.

questions.question: Which islands are used as an example of hot spot volcanoes?
questions.modelAnswer: The Hawaiian Islands.

questions.question: Why are volcanoes common at subduction zones?
questions.modelAnswer: A sinking oceanic plate can help mantle rock melt, forming magma that rises to the surface.

questions.question: What conditions make an underwater earthquake more likely to cause a tsunami?
questions.modelAnswer: It is more likely if the earthquake is strong, shallow, and causes vertical movement of the seafloor.

questions.question: Explain why tsunami waves can be dangerous even if they are low in the deep ocean.
questions.modelAnswer: In deep ocean they can travel fast and be low, but near shore they slow down, pile up, grow taller, and create flooding and strong currents.

data.sourcePassage: A natural hazard is a natural event that could harm people, property, or the environment. A hazard becomes a disaster when it causes serious harm. The amount of damage depends not only on the event, but also on exposure, vulnerability, and preparedness. A coastal town near a subduction zone may need to prepare for earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides, and volcanoes if volcanoes are nearby. Scientists collect data such as fault maps, GPS motion, small earthquakes, gas changes, ground swelling, and warning buoy records. Engineers and communities reduce risk with stronger building codes, flexible pipes, hazard maps, evacuation routes, warning systems, emergency drills, and careful planning about where to build. Mitigation cannot stop plate motion, but it can reduce danger.

questions.question: When does a hazard become a disaster?
questions.modelAnswer: It becomes a disaster when it causes serious harm.

questions.question: Which is a mitigation strategy from the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Stronger building codes.

questions.question: Name two types of data scientists can collect to study hazard risk.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include fault maps, GPS motion, small earthquakes, gas changes, ground swelling, and warning buoy records.

questions.question: Why is preparedness important if scientists cannot stop plate motion?
questions.modelAnswer: Preparedness reduces harm by helping people build safer structures, plan evacuations, respond quickly, and avoid the highest-risk areas.

questions.question: Explain how the same hazard could create different risk in two communities.
questions.modelAnswer: Risk differs because communities may have different exposure, building quality, population density, warning systems, emergency plans, and resources.
